1.pericope_label: And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out against the Philistines to battle, and pitched beside Eben-ezer: and the Philistines pitched in Aphek

schools.summary: Henry begins by detaching the opening clause from the story that follows. The first words, which relate to Samuel, that his word came to all Israel, seem not to have any reference to the following narrative, as if it was by any direction of his that the Israelites went out against the Philistines. Had they consulted him, though but newly initiated as a prophet, his counsel might have stood them in more stead than the presence of the ark did; but perhaps the princes of Israel despised his youth and would not have recourse to him as an oracle, and he did not as yet interpose in public affairs, nor is there any further mention of his name until some years later. What the clause means, then, is that people from all parts who were piously disposed had recourse to him as a prophet and consulted him; or perhaps it refers to his prophecy against the house of Eli, which was generally known and talked of, so that all who were serious and observing compared the events here related, when they came to pass, with the prophecy, and saw it accomplished in them. Of the war itself Henry says it was an attempt to throw off the yoke of Philistine oppression, and would have succeeded better if they had first repented and reformed, and so begun their work at the right end. He gives the two datings that had been proposed: Bishop Patrick computes that this was about the middle of the forty years' dominion of the Philistines and soon after the death of Samson, whose slaughter at his death might have encouraged the attempt, whereas Dr. Lightfoot reckons it forty years after Samson's death, for so long Eli judged. Of the defeat Henry notes only that Israel, who were the aggressors, were smitten, and four thousand killed upon the spot: God had promised that one of them should chase a thousand, but now, on the contrary, Israel is smitten before the Philistines, for sin, the accursed thing, was in the camp, and gave their enemies all the advantage against them they could wish for.

Ellicott sets out the question of the opening clause at length. To which portion of the narrative does the statement belong? Is it part of the account of the Lord's dealings with Samuel which closed the preceding chapter, closing that brief narrative of the divine voice and the vision with a note simply relating how the word of the boy-prophet was received through the varied tribes? Or does it tell us that at Samuel's word — that is, acting under his advice — Israel commenced this new disastrous war? Adopting the first supposition removes the grave difficulty of supposing that Samuel was mistaken in his first advice to the people; but then we have to explain the separation of the clause from the preceding section to which it seems so naturally to belong, and to account for the exceeding abruptness with which the announcement of the war follows. Ellicott notes the suggestion of the Speaker's Commentary, that the account of the battle was extracted from some other book where it came in consecutively, and was introduced here to exhibit the fulfilment of Samuel's prophecy concerning Eli's family; but he observes that the Hebrew revisers evidently did not so understand it, having placed the notice of Samuel's words as introducing the narrative of the battle. He then sets the young prophet's error in its historical frame. Anarchy and confusion had long prevailed throughout the tribes, and none of the hero Judges raised to power had succeeded in restoring the stern, rigid form of theocracy which had made the Israel of Moses and Joshua so great; the high qualities which in his prime had raised Eli to the first place were in his old age almost totally obscured by a weak affection for his unworthy sons, and a terrible picture of the corruption of the priesthood belongs to the last period of his rule. In that state of moral degradation the Philistines, part of the original inhabitants of the land, a warlike and enterprising race, took advantage of the internal jealousies and weaknesses of Israel and made themselves supreme in many portions of the land. Samuel grew up in the midst of this, conscious that the invisible King had chosen him to be the restorer of the chosen people, but he does not appear at first to have recognised the depth of the degradation, or to have seen that it was utterly hopeless to free the people from the Philistine yoke until something like a pure national religion was restored; so the first call to arms resulted in utter disaster, and the defeat at Aphek was the prelude to the crushing blow which soon deprived Israel of their leaders, their choicest warriors, and above all of their cherished Ark. Of the place-name Ellicott notes that it means the stones of help and was not given until Samuel set up a stone to commemorate a victory some twenty years later, and that the other name carries the article, the fortress, perhaps the old Canaanite royal city. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the whole chapter at the outset — the attack and defeat, the fetching of the ark, the greater defeat in which Eli's sons fell and the ark was taken, the death of Eli, and the death of his daughter-in-law — and read the disaster as a double lesson: the people were to learn that the Lord had departed from them, and Samuel also was to make the discovery that the deliverance of Israel from the oppression of its foes was absolutely impossible without its inward conversion.

Clarke opens with the chapter in summary and then makes one decisive textual judgment: the clause about the word of Samuel certainly belongs to the preceding chapter, and is so placed by the Vulgate, the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Arabic. On the place where the camp was pitched he observes that the name was not given to it until more than twenty years after this battle, since the monument called the Stone of Help was erected by Samuel in the place afterwards so called, when the Lord had given the Israelites a signal victory over the Philistines; it was situated in the tribe of Judah, between Mizpeh and Shen, and not far from the Aphek here mentioned. This, he adds, is another proof that the book was compiled after the times and transactions which it records, and probably from memoranda which had been made by a contemporary writer. Wesley takes the other side of the disputed clause, understanding it of the word of the Lord revealed to Samuel and by him to the people — a word of command that all Israel should go forth to fight with the Philistines, as the following words explain it, that they might first be humbled and punished for their sins, and so prepared for deliverance. Of the enemy he adds that the Philistines, having by this time recruited themselves after their loss by Samson, and perceiving an eminent prophet arising among the Israelites by whom they were likely to be united and assisted, thought fit to suppress them in the beginning of their hopes.

Gill allows the clause more than one sense and does not choose between them. It may mean that the word of prophecy by Samuel, which related to what befell Eli and his family, was made known — as the Targum has it — and spread throughout the land, so that almost everyone had knowledge of it, and it began to be fulfilled in the war with the Philistines afterwards related. Or it may mean that the doctrine, instructions and exhortations of Samuel to the people of Israel were by the means of others conveyed throughout the land, and yet they went into measures which proved fatal and ruinous to them. Or, thirdly, it may mean that the word of Samuel, which was from the Lord, came to Israel to stir them up to go to war with the Philistines, whereby the punishment threatened to Eli's family would begin to have its accomplishment.

2.pericope_label: Israel was smitten before the Philistines, and they slew of the army about four thousand men; let us fetch the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of Shiloh unto us

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch attend closely to the Hebrew of the account of the loss. The Israelites were defeated, and four thousand men were smitten in battle-array, the phrase meaning upon the field of battle and not in flight, and the field meaning the open country where the battle was fought. Of the council that followed they say that on the return of the people to the camp the elders held a council of war as to the cause of the defeat they had suffered, asking why Jehovah had smitten them that day before the Philistines. Since they had entered upon the war by the word and advice of Samuel, they were convinced that it was Jehovah who had smitten them; and the question presupposes at the same time both that the Israelites felt strong enough to enter upon the war with their enemies, and that the reason for their defeat could only be that the Lord, their covenant God, had withdrawn his help. This, Keil and Delitzsch grant, was no doubt a correct conclusion; but the means which they adopted to secure the help of their God in continuing the war were altogether wrong, since instead of feeling remorse and seeking the help of the Lord their God they sent for the outward symbol. Ellicott reaches the same judgment from the other end. The people and the elders, who had undertaken the war of liberty at the instigation of the young man of God, were amazed at their defeat and puzzled to understand why God was evidently not in their midst; and they showed by their next procedure how thoroughly they had gone astray from the old pure religion. Whether Samuel acquiesced in the fatal proposition we have no information, but it evidently did not emanate from him; we are expressly told that it came from the elders of the people, and Ellicott conjectures that the lesson of the first defeat had already impressed Samuel deeply, and that he saw a thorough reformation throughout the land was needed before the invisible King would again be present among them. He calls the hope of the elders a curious delusion, this baseless notion that the unseen God was inseparably connected with that strange and beautiful symbol of his presence, a coffer of perishable wood and metal overshadowed by the lifeless golden angels carved on the shining seat which closed it. Far on in the people's story, he adds, one of the greatest of Samuel's successors presses home the same truth the people were so slow in learning, when Jeremiah passionately urges his Israel to trust not in lying words, saying, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord; and Ellicott quotes Wordsworth's observation that David probably remembered this history when, with a clearer faith, he refused to allow the Ark to be carried with him in his retreat before Absalom, and, when the priests had brought it forth, commanded them to carry it back to its place. David, without the Ark visibly present but with the unseen help of him who was enthroned on the mercy-seat, triumphed and was restored to Jerusalem; Israel, with the Ark visibly present but without the blessing of him whose throne it was, fell before their enemies and were deprived of the sacred symbol.

Clarke makes two remarks on the battle and one on the remedy proposed. There is no doubt, he says, that both the Philistines and the Israelites had what might be called the art of war, according to which they marshalled their troops in the field, constructed their camps, and conducted their retreats and sieges, though we do not know the principles on which they acted. And this must have been a severe conflict, since four thousand were left dead on the field of battle; the contest also must have lasted some considerable time, as these were all slain hand to hand, swords and spears being in all probability the only weapons then in use. On the proposal to fetch the ark he is severe: they vainly supposed that it could save them, when the God of it had departed from them because of their wickedness. They knew that in former times their fathers had been beaten by their enemies when they did not take the ark with them to battle, as in the case of their wars with the Canaanites, and that they had conquered when they took it with them, as in the case of the destruction of Jericho; from the latter clause they took confidence, but the cause of their miscarriage in the former they laid not to heart. Clarke adds that it was customary with all the nations of the earth to take their gods and sacred ensigns with them to war — the Persians, Indians, Greeks, Romans, Germans and Philistines did so — and that consecrated crosses, and the blessing and hallowing of colours and standards, are the modern remains of those ancient superstitions. Wesley calls the elders' question strange blindness: when there was so great a corruption in their worship and manners, they could not see sufficient reason why God should suffer them to fall by their enemies. Of the ark he says they took it for that great pledge of God's presence and help by whose conduct their ancestors obtained success; and instead of humbling themselves for, and purging themselves from, the sins for which God was displeased with them, they take an easier and cheaper course and put their trust in their ceremonial observances, not doubting but the very presence of the ark would give them the victory.

Gill describes the two moments briefly. The Philistines prepared for battle and put themselves in a posture for it, forming themselves in a line of battle, and so inviting and challenging the Israelites to fight them; and when the people came into the camp, it was at Eben-ezer, where they had pitched their tents and from whence they went out to battle, and whither they returned after their defeat.

4.pericope_label: They brought from Shiloh the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts; all Israel shouted with a great shout, so that the earth rang again, and the Philistines heard the noise

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the errand against the memory that prompted it. There was, no doubt, in the minds of the elders the memory of many a glorious victory gained in the old heroic days of Moses and Joshua in the presence of their sacred Ark; but then God was with his people, and the Ark of the Covenant served as a reminder of his ever-presence with them, whereas now they had been disloyal to their unseen King, his very sanctuary had become infamous as the centre of vice, his ministers were chiefly known as the prominent examples of covetousness and immorality, and the Ark had become only a symbol of the broken covenant. It was in vain that the grand battle hymn of Israel was raised as in the old days when the Ark set forward, Rise up, Lord, and let thine enemies be scattered. The notice that the two sons of Eli were there with the Ark, Ellicott finds sufficient by itself to account for the terrible discomfiture of Israel; what a contrast the writer bitterly puts down in his memoirs here, between the glorious but now deserted earthly throne of God and its guardians, the wicked, abandoned priests. Of the shout he observes that, as far as we know, this was the first time since the establishment of the people in Canaan that the Ark had been brought from the permanent sanctuary into the camp, and that the shout of joy represented the confidence of the army that now the Ark, which had witnessed so many splendid victories of the chosen race, was among them, discomfiture was out of the question. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of both points: on the arrival of the ark the people raised so great a shout of joy that the earth rang again, this being probably the first time since the settlement in Canaan that the ark had been brought into the camp, so that the people no doubt anticipated from its presence a renewal of the marvellous victories gained by Israel under Moses and Joshua. When the Philistines heard the noise and learned on inquiry that the ark of Jehovah had come into the camp, they were thrown into alarm, saying that God was come into the camp, and crying woe unto us, for such a thing has not happened yesterday or the day before; who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? They spoke of the God of Israel in the plural, as heathen who only knew of gods and not of one Almighty God; and just as all the heathen feared in a certain degree the might of the gods of other nations, so the Philistines were alarmed at the might of the God of the Israelites.

Clarke explains the notion the elders were working on. Of what shape the cherubim were we do not know, but one of these representative figures was placed at each end of the ark of the covenant, and between them, on the lid or cover of that ark, which was called the propitiatory or mercy-seat, the shechinah, or symbol of the divine presence, was said to dwell; they thought therefore that if they had the ark, they must necessarily have the presence and influence of Jehovah. On the shout that greeted its arrival he is short and severe: had they humbled themselves, and prayed devoutly and fervently for success, they would have been heard and saved, whereas their shouting proved both their vanity and their irreligion. Wesley reads the shout as coming from their great joy and confidence of success, and turns it into a warning to his own readers: so formal Christians triumph in external privileges and performances, as if the ark in the camp would bring them to heaven, though the world and the flesh reign in the heart.

Gill follows the sequence plainly: the people liked the proposal of the elders, took their advice, and joined with them in a message to Eli the high priest at Shiloh; the ark came into the camp, being brought thither by the men that carried it; and the shout that greeted it was so loud as to make the earth ring, and so was heard in the camp of the Philistines, which may not have been at any great distance from the camp of Israel, though how far Aphek and Eben-ezer stood from each other is not certain.

7.pericope_label: The Philistines were afraid, for they said, God is come into the camp; who shall deliver us out of the hand of these mighty Gods? Be strong, and quit yourselves like men

schools.summary: Ellicott explains what the Philistines inferred and why they were entitled to fear it. The joy manifested by the Israelites at the arrival of the Ark from the sanctuary made them suspect that their enemies' God was now present with the defeated army; and Philistines and Israelites alike were equally superstitious in their belief, both supposing that Deity was in some way connected with the lifeless gold and wood of the symbol. But the Philistines had some excuse for their fears, since tradition was no doubt current among the old inhabitants of Canaan how this sacred Ark had been carried before the conquering armies of Israel in many a battle and siege in those bygone days when the strange shepherd hordes under Joshua first invaded and took possession of their beautiful land. He locates the ground as well: the city of Aphek, near to which the camp of Israel was pitched, stood close to the western entrance of the Pass of Beth-horon, and the two defeats of Israel may be termed the battles of Aphek. Of the cry that follows he takes the words to be the very words of the Philistines, preserved in their national traditions of this sad time, and the expression of idolaters who knew of gods and dreaded their malevolent influence but had no conception of the One Most High God. The plural form so often found in the sacred record for God is used here; but whereas the inspired compilers would have written the qualifying adjective in the singular, the Philistine idolaters write theirs in the plural, mighty gods. It is noticeable, Ellicott adds, that the exclamation of awe and terror is based outwardly upon the Egyptian traditions of the acts of the Lord, and that they studiedly ignore what they were all in that camp painfully conscious of, his acts in their own land of Canaan. The Septuagint and Syriac, and some commentators, insert a word before the mention of the wilderness to make the exclamation more in harmony with history, seeing that the plagues were inflicted before the Israelites entered the wilderness; but the very vagueness of the exclamation of fear speaks for its truth, since they were little concerned with exact historical accuracy, and were simply conscious of some terrible judgment having fallen on the foes of this Israel, a judgment they not unnaturally connected with the Ark just arrived in the enemy's camp. Of the rallying cry Ellicott says its ring — part of the same Philistine tradition of their splendid success, and probably embodied in some well-known hymn of victory — was evidently in Paul's mind when he wrote his stirring words of exhortation to the Corinthian Church, quit ye like men, be strong. Keil and Delitzsch note only that instead of despairing they encouraged one another, saying, show yourselves strong and be men, O Philistines, that we may not be obliged to serve the Hebrews as they have served you.

Clarke states the Philistine error in a sentence: they took for granted, as did the Israelites, that the presence of God was inseparable from his ark or shrine. On the cry that follows he would render the Hebrew in the singular rather than the plural — who shall deliver us from the hand of this illustrious God? — thinking that probably the true sense. Of the rallying cry he expands the threat that lay behind it, and finds it very forcible: if ye do not fight and acquit yourselves like men, ye will be servants to the Hebrews as they have been to you, and you may expect that they will avenge themselves of you for all the cruelty you have exercised towards them. Wesley narrows the words there hath not been such a thing heretofore to mean not in our times, since the earlier removals of the ark took place before it came to rest at Shiloh. Of the cry itself he observes that they secretly confess the Lord to be greater than their gods, and yet presume to oppose him; and of the difficulty about the wilderness he offers a solution, that they mention it not as if all the plagues of the Egyptians came upon them there, but because the last and sorest of all, which is therefore put for all, the destruction of Pharaoh and all his host, happened in the wilderness, namely in the Red Sea, which, having the wilderness on both sides of it, may well be said to be in the wilderness. He adds that it is not strange if these heathen mistook some circumstance in the relation of Israelitish affairs, especially some hundreds of years after they were done.

Gill supplies the small connecting facts and one note on the plural. The Philistines were afraid when the spies returned and reported to them the reason of the shouting. Of the cry, who shall deliver us out of the hand of these mighty gods, he suggests they may have spoken in an ironical and sneering manner; or, if seriously and through fear, they used their own heathenish language, as if the Israelites had many gods, as they themselves had, though mightier than theirs. He notes that the Syriac and Arabic versions read in the singular, out of the hand of God, or of the most strong God, and that the Targum has, out of the hand of the Word of the Lord. Of the rallying cry he observes that this was all they had to depend upon, their manly courage; if they did not exert it, it was all over with them, and seeing their case was desperate, having gods as well as men to fight with, it became them to exert themselves to the uttermost, which, if they did, there was still a possibility of gaining victory and immortal honour. These words, Gill thinks, seem to be spoken by the generals and officers of the army of the Philistines to the common soldiers.

10.pericope_label: Israel was smitten, and there fell thirty thousand footmen; and the ark of God was taken, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were slain

schools.summary: Ellicott traces the outcome to what he calls the immutable laws which have ever guided the connection of Israel and their God-Friend. As long as they clave to the invisible Preserver, and served him with their whole heart and soul, and kept themselves pure from the pollution of the idol nations around them, so long was he in their midst, and so long would they be invincible; but if, as now, they chose to revel in the impure joys and to delight themselves in the selfish, shameless lives of the idolatrous world around them, and only carried the Ark on their shoulders with no memory in their hearts of him whom the mercy-seat and the overshadowing cherubim symbolised, then, in the solemn words of the hymn of Asaph, God was wroth and greatly abhorred Israel, and forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, and delivered his strength into captivity and his glory into the enemy's hand. Of the capture itself Ellicott notes that the bare fact is given without comment or note, though it was the greatest calamity that had yet happened to Israel; all the people would know by this terrible sign that their invisible King had withdrawn his countenance from them, but the loss of the Ark to the heathen taught another lesson besides, not merely for the Israel of the days of Eli and Samuel — the eternal truth that the living God does not bind his presence to a dead thing. And though it was a dead thing, it was inexpressibly precious to the patriot Israelite: was it not the ark which Moses had made by God's command at Sinai, and on which the divine presence was enshrined in the Holy of Holies, which had accompanied Israel in their marches through the wilderness, and before which the waters of Jordan had fled backward and the walls of Jericho had fallen down — that ark was taken by idolaters. Of the death of the priests he says only that it was in strict accordance with the saying of the man of God. Keil and Delitzsch take the two losses together as a practical proof to the degenerate nation that Jehovah, who was enthroned above the cherubim, had departed from them, that is, had withdrawn his gracious presence; and they draw the lesson forward, that it is just the same now when we take merely a historical Christ outside us for our Redeemer, since he must prove his help chiefly internally by his Holy Spirit, though externally he must not be thrown into the shade as accomplishing our justification.

Henry sets the rout under three heads, each of them a thing that might have been expected to prevent it. Israel was put to the worse though they had the better cause, being the people of God while the Philistines were uncircumcised, and standing up in necessary defence of their just rights and liberties against invaders; and yet they failed of success, for their rock had sold them — a good cause often suffers for the sake of the bad men that undertake it. They were put to the worse though they had the greater confidence and were the more courageous, since they shouted while the Philistines trembled, and yet, when God pleased so to order it, the Philistines' terrors were turned into triumphs and Israel's shouts into lamentations. And they were put to the worse though they had the ark of God with them, since external privileges will secure none that abuse them and do not live up to them, and the ark in the camp will add nothing to its strength when there is an Achan in it. The dispersal was final: they did not retire into the camp, as after the first defeat when they hoped to rally again, but returned to their tents, every man shifting for his own safety and making the best of his way home, despairing to make head any more. Of the death of Eli's sons Henry says that, considering their bad character, it was no great loss to Israel, but a dreadful judgment upon the house of Eli, in which the word already spoken was fulfilled, that his two sons should die both in one day. Had Eli done his duty and put them, as polluted, from the priesthood, they might have lived, though in disgrace; but now God takes the work into his own hands and chases them out of the world by the sword of the uncircumcised. They were out of their place, Henry adds — what had they to do in the camp? — and when men leave the way of their duty they shut themselves out of God's protection; but this was not all, for they had betrayed the ark by bringing it into danger without a warrant from God, and this filled the measure of their iniquities. The taking of the ark was a very great judgment upon Israel and a certain token of God's displeasure: now they are made to see their folly in trusting to external privileges which their wickedness had forfeited, and to reflect with the utmost regret upon their own rashness in bringing the ark into the camp and so exposing it; now they are convinced that God will not be prescribed to by vain and foolish men, and that though he has bound us to his ark he has not bound himself to it, but will rather deliver it into the hands of his sworn enemies than suffer it to be profaned by his false friends.

Wesley marks the arithmetic of the two defeats: before, they lost but four thousand; now, in the presence of the ark, thirty thousand — to teach them that the ark and the ordinances of God were never designed as a refuge to impenitent sinners, but only for the comfort of those that repent. He explains the phrase that every man fled into his tent as meaning to his habitation, called by the ancient name of his tent. Of the capture of the ark he gives four reasons why God justly and wisely permitted it: to punish the Israelites for their profanation of it; that by taking away the pretences of their foolish confidence he might more deeply humble them and bring them to true repentance; that the Philistines might by this means be more effectually convinced of God's almighty power and of the impotency of their own gods; and so that a stop might be put to their triumphs and rage against the poor Israelites. Thus, as God was no loser by this event, so the Philistines were no gainers by it, and Israel, all things considered, received more good than hurt by it. Of Eli's sons Wesley repeats that if Eli had done his duty and put them from the priesthood they might have lived, though in disgrace, but that now God takes the work into his own hands and chases them out of the world by the sword of the Philistines. Clarke adds only that they probably attempted to defend the ark and lost their lives in the attempt.

Gill notes that the Philistines fought with great ardour and spirit, quitting themselves like men of valour and courage, their case being desperate as they imagined, since God was in the camp of Israel. Of the capture he gives two reasons for the permission: partly as a punishment to the Israelites for fetching the ark from the tabernacle without the will of God, and for their vain confidence in it; and partly that the Philistines might have an experiment of the power and might of God, as Procopius Gazaeus observes, by what they would suffer through having it among them. He adds that some have thought this an emblem of Christ being delivered into the hands of the Gentiles, and of the Gospel being translated from the Jews to them.

12.pericope_label: And there ran a man of Benjamin out of the army, and came to Shiloh the same day with his clothes rent, and with earth upon his head

schools.summary: Henry follows the news from the battlefield to Shiloh. Bad news flies fast, and this soon spread through all Israel, every man that fled to his tent bringing it, with too plain a proof of it, to his neighbours; but no place was so nearly concerned as Shiloh, and thither an express posted away immediately. It was a man of Benjamin — the Jews fancy it was Saul — who rent his clothes and put earth upon his head, by these signs to proclaim the sorrowful news to all who saw him as he ran, and to show how much he was himself affected with it. Of the city's reception of the tidings Henry notes that Eli sat in the gate, but the messenger was loath to tell him first, and therefore passed him by and told it in the city with all its aggravating circumstances; and now both the ears of every one that heard it tingled, as had been foretold, their hearts trembled, and every face gathered blackness. All the city cried out, and well they might, for besides that this was a calamity to all Israel it was a particular loss to Shiloh and the ruin of that place: though the ark was soon rescued out of the hands of the Philistines, it never returned to Shiloh again; their candlestick was removed out of its place because they had left their first love, and their city dwindled and sank and came to nothing. Now God forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, they having driven him from them, and the tribe of Ephraim, which had for three hundred and forty years been blessed with the presence of the ark, lost the honour, which some time after was transferred to the tribe of Judah, the Mount Zion which he loved, because the men of Shiloh knew not the day of their visitation. This abandoning of Shiloh, Henry adds, Jerusalem is long afterwards reminded of and told to take warning by: go see what I did to Shiloh; from this fatal day let the desolations of Shiloh be dated. They had therefore reason enough to cry out when they heard that the ark was taken.

Clarke first fixes the distance from the speed of the messenger: the field of battle could not have been at any great distance, since this young man reached Shiloh the same evening after the defeat. He then makes the signs of mourning a study in comparative custom. The rent clothes and the earth upon the head were signs of sorrow and distress among all nations: the clothes rent signified the rending, dividing and scattering of the people; the earth or ashes on the head signified their humiliation — we are brought down to the dust of the earth, we are near to our graves. Clarke then ranges through the poets for the same gestures. In Virgil, Aeneas tears the robe from his shoulders and calls the gods to help when the Trojan fleet is burnt; the queen of King Latinus, resolving on her own death when the Trojans have taken the city by storm, tears with both her hands her purple vest; and Latinus himself, stunned by the fate of his wife and the ruin of his city, tears his garments and defiles his venerable beard and silver hairs with unclean dust. Catullus expresses the same in a single line, dishonouring her hoary locks with earth and sprinkled dust. Clarke notes that the ancient Greeks in their mourning often shaved off their hair, quoting the Odyssey twice, where the rites of woe are to shear the graceful curl and drop the tender tear, and where each of the Danaans clipped the curling honours of his head over the dead; and the image is complete, he says, in the case of Achilles, who, hearing of the death of Patroclus, cast on the ground the scorching ashes over his graceful head, deforming his purple garments with dust and his golden hair with tears. He ends nearer home: it is not unusual, even in Europe and in the most civilized parts of it, to see grief expressed by tearing the hair, beating the breasts and rending the garments, all these being natural signs or expressions of deep and excessive grief, and common to all the nations of the world.

Ellicott reports the Rabbinical tradition that this messenger was Saul, who snatched from Goliath the tables of the Law taken out of the Ark, in order to save them, and then turns from the legend to the quality of the narrative: the whole of this account is so vivid, and so full of detail, that it must have come from some eye-witness — probably from Samuel himself. He observes that such swift runners are still employed to carry news in war time in the East, and collects the notable instances. In the sacred story, Cushi and Ahimaaz bring the tidings from Joab to King David after Absalom's death; Asahel, the son of Zeruiah the sister of David, is mentioned as being famous for his running; Elijah once outran the chariot of Ahab between Carmel and Jezreel. Outside it, Phidippides, when sent to urge the people of Sparta to come to the help of the Athenians against the Persians, arrived at Sparta on the second day after his departure from Athens, as Herodotus relates. Running, Ellicott concludes, seems to have been an exercise specially cultivated among the athletes of old times. Of the messenger's appearance he adds only that the rent clothes and the earth upon the head were the usual indications that the news he brought was tidings of evil.

Gill notices that the man ran out of the rank in which he was, before the whole army was quite broken up. He takes him for a young man, as Josephus says, which he thinks highly probable; but what the Jews say, that this was Saul, later king of Israel, he judges not at all to be depended on.

13.pericope_label: Eli sat upon a seat by the wayside watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God; and all the city cried out. Now Eli was ninety and eight years old

schools.summary: Ellicott would render the description of Eli's post more exactly than our version: Eli sat by the side of the way of the watchers, that is, the street or way in Shiloh so named probably from the watch-tower situated in it, while the Septuagint has it, by the side of the gate watching the way. The old judge was naturally anxious for news from the army, since the people had already suffered a great reverse in the first battle when four thousand fell; but his chief anxiety was for that sacred Ark which he had allowed — no doubt against his better judgment — to leave the sanctuary. All had gone wrong lately, and the high priest was deeply conscious that he, for his part, with his culpable weakness, and his priestly sons, with their flagrant wickedness, had broken the covenant with the invisible King. Ellicott credits Eli with more insight than the elders had: he knew too much of the Eternal Guardian of Israel to put any real trust in the power of the lifeless Ark, and knew well how long it was since the glory had rested on its golden mercy-seat between the silent cherubim — had that mysterious light shone in the dark Holy of Holies since the night when the divine voice spoke to the child? So he waited with sorrowful forebodings the advent of the messenger, asking himself whether the Ark would ever return to Shiloh. Of the moment of the arrival Ellicott fills in the scene: the blind old man seated on his chair of state, surrounded by priests and Levites in attendance on him as high priest and judge; as the runner drew near and the torn dress and the dust sprinkled on his head became visible, the wail of woe would soon run through the place, and that cry of sorrow was the first intimation to the blind Eli. His question was probably, in the first place, addressed to the little court standing by his throne; and the narrative is so vivid that we seem to hear the cries of grief and terror which Eli heard, and to see the scene of dismay and confusion which those sightless eyes were prevented from looking on. On the note of his age Ellicott adds a caution about numbers generally: the Septuagint reads ninety years here and the Syriac seventy-eight, and where numbers are concerned we usually find these varieties of translation and interpretation, since the Hebrews used the letters of the alphabet to express numbers, a system naturally fruitful in errors of transcription, so that numbers and dates especially in the earlier books are frequently confused and uncertain, and many of the difficulties which have given commentators so much trouble have arisen out of copyists inadvertently substituting one letter for another. Instead of "his eyes were dim" the more accurate rendering would be, his eyes were set, were stiff, so that he could no longer see — a description, as Keil observes, of the so-called black cataract, which not infrequently occurs at a very great age from paralysis of the optic nerves. Of the messenger's opening words Ellicott notes that the fatal battle had taken place very early that same morning, that the very words of the runner were remembered, and that the whole vivid scene was evidently related by a bystander, some having even suggested that it was Samuel who stood by Eli's side. Keil and Delitzsch give the same reading of the eyes and the same diagnosis of the condition.

Gill supposes that the runner either passed by Eli, who being blind could not see him, or came in at another gate of the city on the other side of it, as Abarbinel thinks; the former seems the more likely, since he did not choose to deliver the bad news to Eli first, knowing how much it would grieve him, and therefore slipped by him into the city. Of Eli's hearing the outcry Gill observes that he had his hearing, though not his sight: he could not see the distress in their countenances, but he heard the shrieks of the men and women, which were very clamorous and terrible. Of the note of his age he says it is very properly observed at this point, Eli being now come to the end of his days, and that it also accounts for the blindness afterwards mentioned. And of the messenger's approach he judges it very probable that the people Eli inquired of told him there was a messenger come from the army, though they did not choose to relate to him the news he brought.

Clarke fixes on the paradox in Eli's fear: he was a most mild and affectionate father, and yet the safety of the ark lay nearer to his heart than the safety of his two sons — who can help feeling for this aged, venerable man? Wesley reads the same trembling as the discovery of a public and generous spirit, and a fervent zeal for God and for his honour, which Eli preferred before all his natural affections, not regarding his own children in comparison of the ark, though otherwise he was a most indulgent father. He adds, of the outcry of the city, that they might well cry out, for besides that this was a calamity to all Israel it was a particular loss to Shiloh, since the ark never returned thither; their candlestick was removed out of its place, and the city sank and came to nothing.

17.pericope_label: Israel is fled before the Philistines, thy two sons also are dead, and the ark of God is taken; and Eli fell from off the seat backward, and his neck brake, and he died

schools.summary: Clarke says never was a more afflictive message, containing such a variety of woes, each rising above the preceding, delivered in so few words, and takes the four clauses in order. Israel is fled before the Philistines: this was a sore evil, that Israel should turn their backs upon their enemies, and worse that they should turn them upon such enemies as these, for now they might expect the chains of their slavery to be strengthened and riveted more closely. There hath also been a great slaughter among the people: a rout might have taken place without any great previous slaughter, but in this case the field was warmly contested and thirty thousand were laid dead on the spot, so that it was as if he had said, the flower of our armies is destroyed, scarcely a veteran now to take the field. Thy two sons are dead: this was still more afflictive to him as a father, to lose both his sons, the only hope of the family, and to have them taken away by a violent death when there was so little prospect of their having died in the peace of God. And the ark of God is taken: this was the most dreadful of the whole, for now Israel is dishonoured in the sight of the heathen and the name of the Lord will be blasphemed by them; besides, the capture of the ark shows that God is departed from Israel. How high does each woe rise on the back of the preceding, Clarke exclaims, and with what apparent art is this very laconic message constructed — and yet probably no art at all was used, and the messenger delivered the tidings just as the facts rose up in his own mind. He sets it against the messenger's speech in the Persae of Aeschylus, which brings the queen the tremendous account of the destruction of the whole naval power of the Persians at Salamis, and which he finds vapid and diffuse by comparison, being only the sum of an account afterwards detailed in a dozen speeches. He sets it also against three celebrated brevities of commanders: the three words in which Julius Caesar reported to the Roman senate his total defeat of Pharnaces, king of Pontus, a war begun and ended in one day; the sentence in which Admiral Hawke told King George that he had taken, burnt and destroyed all the French fleet, as per margin; and the note Bonaparte, then general-in-chief in Italy, sent his wife the evening before he attacked Field Marshal Alvinzi, promising that he would attack the enemy, defeat them, and terminate the business — which he did. In each of these, excellent as they are in their kind, we find little more than one idea, whereas the report of the Benjamite includes several, pointing out in the most forcible manner the general and particular disasters of the day, the rout of the army, the great slaughter, the death of the priests who were in effect the whole generals of the army, and the capture of the ark; and all this he does in four simple assertions. Of Eli's fall Clarke says he bore all the relation till the messenger came to that solemn word: he had trembled before for the ark, and now, hearing that it was captured, he was transfixed with grief, fell down from his seat, and dislocated his neck. Yet Clarke will not have him counted lost: shall we say that this man, however remiss in the education of his children, and criminal in his indulgence towards his profligate sons — which arose more from the easiness of his disposition than from a desire to encourage vice — is gone to perdition? God forbid; no man ever died with such benevolent and religious feelings and yet perished. He notes that the Septuagint has twenty years for the length of his rule, while all the other versions and the Hebrew text have forty. Wesley describes the fall itself: he was so oppressed with grief and astonishment that he had no strength left to support him; he sat by the gate of the city, which was most convenient for the speedy understanding of all occurrences; he was old, and therefore weak and apt to fall, and heavy, and therefore his fall the more dangerous. So fell the high priest and judge of Israel, so fell his heavy head when he had lived within two of a hundred years, so fell the crown from his head when he had judged Israel forty years, and thus did his sun set under a cloud; thus was the wickedness of those sons of his whom he had indulged his ruin, and thus does God sometimes set marks of his displeasure on good men, that others may hear and fear. Yet Wesley too insists that it was the loss of the ark that was his death, and not the slaughter of his sons: he says in effect, let me fall with the ark — who can live when the ordinances of God are removed? Farewell all in this world, even life itself, if the ark be gone.

Keil and Delitzsch narrate the collapse plainly: when the messenger informed him of the defeat of the Israelites, the death of his sons, and the capture of the ark, at the last news Eli fell back from his seat by the side of the gate, and broke his neck, and died; the loss of the ark was to him the most dreadful of all, more dreadful than the death of his two sons. Of the length of his rule they say the reading twenty in the Septuagint does not deserve the slightest notice, if only because it is perfectly incredible that Eli should have been appointed judge of the nation in his seventy-eighth year. Ellicott draws an argument from the character of the compiler. He was actuated by no feeling of friendship to the high priest Eli, and in composing this history of the events which led to the elevation of Samuel he simply puts together the materials he possessed, giving a vivid picture of the calamities of Eli's rule; and as he never spares his weakness, or attempts to veil his blind nepotism, we feel here the perfect truth of the touching incident which closed the old man's life. He loved the Ark, because of its close connection with his God, better after all than his two sons: he could bear the stern announcement of the ruin and degradation of the fortunes of his proud house, for which he had toiled only too faithfully; he could bear to see another, the boy Samuel, preferred before him, the high priest and judge of Israel; he could endure to hear of the defeat and ruin of the country over which he had so long ruled and which he loved so well; even the news of the death of his sons he could listen to with sad resignation; but when his ears caught the words that the ark of God was taken, the old man's heart broke and he died. The chronicler of this period, who certainly never favoured Eli, leaves upon us the impression that with all his faults and imperfections he was still a servant of God; and Ellicott quotes with Wordsworth the psalm which says, if I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning, and recalls that the dying words of Archbishop Whitgift were, for the church of God. On the note that Eli had judged Israel forty years he quotes at length Bishop Sanderson's reflection that, when he reads of Eli the priest judging Israel so long, and of Samuel going circuit as a judge itinerant, and of others of the families of Levi appointed by David to be judges and officers not only in all the business of the Lord but also for the outward business of Israel, and observes how ever since the world had Christian princes ecclesiastical persons have been employed by their sovereigns in their weightiest affairs of state, he cannot but wonder at those who inveigh against the courts, power, jurisdiction and temporalities of bishops.

Gill commends the messenger's method: he delivered his account gradually, beginning with generals and then proceeding to particulars, and with what he thought Eli could better bear the news of, and so prepared him for the worst — in which he acted a wise part. Of the fall he says that when the man made mention of the ark of God, of the taking of that, it struck Eli to the heart and killed him; the rest he bore tolerably well, the flight of Israel before the Philistines, the great slaughter made of them, the death of his two sons; but the taking of the ark was so dreadful to him that he could not support under it.

19.pericope_label: The wife of Phinehas travailed and bowed herself; and she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory is departed from Israel: for the ark of God is taken

schools.summary: Henry calls this another melancholy story, carrying on the desolations of Eli's house, and concerning the wife of Phinehas, one of those ungracious sons who had brought all this mischief on Israel. It cost her her life, though young, as well as that of her father-in-law, who was old; for many a green head, as well as many a hoary head, has been brought by sorrow to the grave. He finds in her two things. First, that she was a woman of a very tender spirit. Providence so ordered it that just at this time she was near her time, and the amazing news, coming at this unhappy juncture, put her into labour, as great frights or other strong passions sometimes do; when she heard of the death of her father-in-law whom she reverenced, and her husband whom, bad as he was, she loved, but especially of the loss of the ark, she travailed, for her pains came thickly upon her, and the tidings so seized her spirits, at a time when they needed all possible supports, that though she had strength to bear the child she soon after fainted and died away, being very willing to let life go when she had lost the greatest comforts of her life. Those who are drawing near to that trying hour, Henry adds, have need to treasure up for themselves comforts from the covenant of grace, to balance not only the usual sorrows but anything extraordinary that may add to a grief they do not foresee. Secondly, that she was a woman of a very gracious spirit, though matched to a wicked husband. Her concern for the death of husband and father-in-law was an evidence of her natural affection, but her much greater concern for the loss of the ark was an evidence of her pious and devout affection to God and sacred things; the former helped to hasten her travail, but it appears by her dying words that the latter lay nearer her heart, since she laments not so much the sinking of the particular family to which she was related as the general calamity of Israel in the captivity of the ark. This made her regardless of her child: the women who attended her, likely some of the first rank in the city, thought her concern was mostly about the issue of her pains, and when the child was born — perhaps her first-born — said unto her, fear not, for thou hast borne a son; but she answered not, neither did she regard it. The sorrows of her travail would have been forgotten for joy that a man-child was born into the world; but what is that joy to one who feels herself dying? No joy but that which is spiritual and divine will stand us in any stead then, for death is too serious a thing to admit the relish of any earthly joy. And what is it to one lamenting the loss of the ark? Small comfort could she have of a child born in Israel, in Shiloh, when the ark is a prisoner in the land of the Philistines. This also made her give the child a name that should perpetuate the remembrance of the calamity and her sense of it: she has nothing to say to the child, only, it being her province now that her husband was dead to name him, she orders them to call him Ichabod — where is the glory, or alas for the glory, or there is no glory — which she explains with her dying lips: the glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God is taken; call the child inglorious, for so he is, the beauty of Israel is lost and there appears no hope of ever retrieving it. Henry draws two notes from it: that the purity and plenty of God's ordinances, and the tokens of his presence in them, are the glory of any people, much more so than their wealth and trade and interest among the nations; and that nothing is more cutting, more killing, to a faithful Israelite than the want and loss of these — if God go, the glory goes, and all good goes.

Clarke calls this another very affecting story: the defeat of Israel, the capture of the ark, the death of her father-in-law and the slaughter of her husband were more than a woman in her circumstances, near the time of her delivery, could bear; she bowed, travailed, was delivered of a son, gave the child a name indicative of the ruined state of Israel, and expired. Of her silence when the women encouraged her he says only that she paid no attention to what they had said concerning her having borne a son — that information she regarded not. On the name he surveys the ancient versions, giving the forms of the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Arabic, and concludes that none of these gives much light on the subject; it is pretty evident they did not know well what signification to give the name, and we are left to collect its meaning from what she says afterwards, that the glory is departed from Israel. The words literally mean, where is the glory — and indeed where was it, Clarke asks, when the armies of Israel were defeated by the Philistines, the priests slain, the supreme magistrate dead, and the ark of the Lord taken? He closes the chapter with a look forward: this is a very eventful, interesting and affecting chapter, and prepares the reader for those signal manifestations of God's power and providence by which the ark was restored, the priesthood re-established, an immaculate judge given to Israel, the Philistine yoke broken, and the people of the Most High caused once more to triumph. God humbled them that he might exalt them; he suffered his glory for a time to become eclipsed, that he might afterwards cause it to break out with the greater effulgence. Wesley, following Henry, grants that the sorrows of her travail would have been forgotten for joy that a child was born into the world, and then asks what that joy is to one who feels herself dying: none but spiritual joy will stand us in stead then, for death admits not the relish of any earthly joy, which is then all flat and tasteless. What is it to one that is lamenting the loss of the ark? What can give us pleasure if we want God's word and ordinances, especially if we want the comfort of his gracious presence and the light of his countenance? Of the repetition of the reason at the last he observes that it is repeated to show her piety, and that the public loss lay heavier upon her spirit than her personal or domestic calamity.

Gill examines the Hebrew of the phrase describing her nearness to delivery. Ben Gersom derives the word from a root which signifies to complete and finish, denoting that her time to bring forth was completed and filled up; Josephus, on the other hand, says that it was a seven months' birth, so that she came two months before her time; and the margin of our Bibles has "to cry out," Moses Kimchi, as his brother relates, deriving the word from a root which signifies to howl and lament, and so expressive of a woman's crying out when her pains come upon her. Of her death he notes that it quickly came on after she was brought to bed. On the name she gave the child, Gill reports that some render it, where is the glory, as in the margin of our Bibles, but that it signifies no glory, as Jarchi and Kimchi interpret it; her husband being dead, it fell to her to give the child its name. And of the last verse he observes that she repeats what she had said before, either for the confirmation of it, or as correcting what the women had said to her.
